title: Dutch elm disease program kept despite provincial cost shift (2016–2018)
summary: When the province shifted the cost of removing diseased elms to municipalities, council chose to keep the Dutch elm disease control program and renewed it each year, and wrote to the Minister of Conservation about its frustration with the change.
status_detail: Agreement approved Jan 19, 2016 and renewed Feb 7, 2017; a provincial Dutch elm grant of $45,207.32 was received in June 2018 (minutes June 19, 2018 item 34).
figures: Extra net cost about $20,000/yr (City Manager, 2016-01-19 0:16:46); 2017 program budget about $35,000 (City Manager, 2017-02-07 0:27:49); provincial grant $45,207.32 (minutes 2018-06-19).
reasons: cost: Not pleased to pay more, but worse not to control the disease. (Michael Zwaagstra)

title: Soccer park washroom and change-room building, plus Community Places grants for parks (2016)
summary: Council applied for provincial Community Places grants for the soccer park building, a BMX pump park and Poplar Park upgrades, and authorized about $370,000 to build long-awaited washrooms and change rooms at the Steinbach Soccer Park before the 2016 Manitoba Summer Games.
status_detail: Building completed by Aug 2016; a $35,000 Community Places grant for it was acknowledged Aug 2, 2016.
figures: Expected cost about $370,000 (City Manager, 2016-03-15 0:08:27); $35,000 grant (mayor, 2016-08-02 0:20:14).

title: Neighbours' noise complaints about a home garage: variance approved, by-law complaints offered as the remedy
summary: Neighbours objected that a rebuilt 1,616 sq ft garage on Quail Ridge had been used for commercial car work with grinding noise and paint fumes. Council approved the size variance, saying noise and home-business problems are handled through existing by-laws if neighbours file complaints.
status_detail: Variance carried (moved by Jac Siemens, seconded by Susan Penner, per transcript). No noise rule changed; administration reported no complaints on file. No follow-up found.
figures: Garage 1,616 sq ft vs 900 sq ft allowed (staff, transcript 0:04:41); zoning by-law s.79.1(f) prohibits home-based vehicle repair (staff, 0:32:27).
reasons: enforcement-limits: Noise and commercial activity can be managed through the complaint process under existing by-laws. (Jac Siemens); enforcement-limits: Asked why neighbours had not complained earlier; said enforcement of commercial activity should be watched. (Deputy Mayor (chair))
public: Neighbours L.K., M.D. and G.K. did not oppose the building but objected to noise, fumes and debris from alleged commercial car work (unproven; the applicant's agent said by-laws provide remedies).
notes: Chair was the Deputy Mayor (addressed 'Mr. Deputy Mayor'); John Fehr was Deputy Mayor (reappointed Nov 1, 2016), but the chair is not named in this video, so no chair quote is used.

title: Council drops the multiplex and makes a downtown performing arts centre conditional on outside funding
summary: After a task force (Susan Penner, Cari Penner, Michael Zwaagstra) reported strong survey support for arts and culture, a Councillor Penner moved principles for recreation planning: a multiplex is not feasible; plan a downtown performing arts centre (PAC) only with adequate parking, other-government funding and 10% private fundraising; seek land for a future arena; keep 1.241 mills for the recreation reserve. Mayor Goertzen objected that this abandoned the master plan.
status_detail: The video ends before the vote; Mayor Goertzen later described an April 2016 'new council resolution and direction to begin development process for the performing arts centre' (2017-07-04 0:21:01), so it appears to have passed.
figures: City tax revenue about $13 million/yr; multiplex studies $100M+ (2012) and $71M (2014); recreation reserve 1.241 mills (motion text, 2016-04-05 part 2 0:45:52).
reasons: cost: A $13M/yr tax base cannot afford a large multiplex even with two-thirds outside funding. (Michael Zwaagstra)
public: Survey and online consultation (2016-03-15) found support for arts and culture; some residents opposed the PAC on cost and parking.

title: Council asks for dog park locations and costs; no city dog park by 2018
summary: Linked to a proposed dog-licence fee increase, council voted unanimously to ask administration for possible dog park locations and costs. Members wanted user fees to cover part of it, no loss of existing parks, and neighbourhood input on location.
status_detail: No location or cost report came back to council in the transcripts to Nov 2018. The 2018 zoning by-law added 'dog park' as a conditional use in park zones (staff, 2018-07-17 1:01:13).
figures: Dog licence revenue under $1,000/yr; 70–80 licences a year (council discussion 2016-06-21 and 2016-08-02).
reasons: cost: Wanted a portion covered by fees, not all from general revenue, and no existing parks used. (Michael Zwaagstra); study-first: Wanted exact cost numbers first. (Earl Funk)
notes: The mover was 'Councillor Penn[er]'; which Penner could not be determined.

title: Canada 150 mosaic mural: residents choose the windmill
summary: For the federally sponsored Canada 150 Mosaic mural, the city collected residents' ideas (including drop boxes at the Soccer Park and Mennonite Heritage Village on Canada Day) and council adopted the windmill, residents' top choice, as the icon. The mural was unveiled with the Community Plaza opening in fall 2016.
status_detail: Windmill adopted Jul 19, 2016; unveiling event listed Nov 1, 2016.

title: Council reaffirms opposition to Manitoba's cosmetic pesticide ban
summary: When the province announced a review of its cosmetic pesticide ban, Michael Zwaagstra moved that the city reaffirm its existing opposition and send its cost information to the province; carried.
status_detail: Carried; the mayor said the position would be submitted to the province.
figures: Organic products would raise lawn-care cost from $18,000 to over $200,000/yr; increased mowing instead costs an extra $30,000–$40,000/yr (Zwaagstra, transcript 1:14:52).
reasons: cost: Ban raises city lawn-care costs and produces more weeds on sports fields and lawns. (Michael Zwaagstra)

title: Welcoming newcomers voiced in council openings; no newcomer, anti-racism or Pride item on the agenda
summary: Councillors spoke about welcoming in meeting openings: John Fehr (Jul 2016) urged a friendlier, more welcoming city, and Earl Funk (Sept 2018) described the Filipino newcomers barbecue and urged welcoming all newcomers. No motion, program, proclamation, flag request, Pride or anti-racism item came before council in the transcripts searched.
status_detail: Statements only; the city's newcomer-related spending found was a $250 grant to the Southeastman Filipino Association in 2017 (R18-065).
figures: $250 grant to Southeastman Filipino Association, 2017 (minutes R18-065).
notes: The first Steinbach Pride march (July 2016) does not appear in any council transcript of this period; no keyword hits for Pride, LGBT, rainbow, racism or multicultural in a council-business sense.

title: Performing arts centre: $7.5M city share, $24.3M estimate, June 30, 2017 deadline, project ended
summary: Council applied for federal-provincial Building Canada funding ($22.5M project) and the Canada Cultural Spaces Fund. When the Class C estimate reached $24.3 million, council split: a Dec 20, 2016 motion reaffirmed the city's $7.5M commitment with a June 30, 2017 sunset. Funding was not secured by the deadline and the project ended in July 2017.
status_detail: Mayor Goertzen announced Jul 4, 2017 that the PAC 'will not move forward in its present form'; council kept setting aside money in a recreation and culture reserve.
figures: City commitment $7.5M; Class C estimate $24.3M (Zwaagstra, 2016-12-20 0:44:53); Building Canada application for $22.5M project (City Manager, 2016-09-06 1:20:56); Canada Cultural Spaces request $5M (2017-02-21 0:24:50); 2017 capital plan $12M PAC in 2017 and 2018 (Zwaagstra, 2017 financial plan hearing 0:16:03); recreation reserve about $750,000 (Zwaagstra, 2017-07-04 0:14:09).
reasons: cost: Did not support a $24M project; doubted matching provincial funds. (Michael Zwaagstra); cost: Feared borrowing; later cited the process and closed meetings. (Earl Funk); provincial-responsibility: Project depended on federal, provincial and private funding that did not arrive by the deadline. (Chris Goertzen)
vote: Dec 20, 2016 sunset motion carried, divided (against: Zwaagstra, Funk, one Councillor Penner)
notes: Speaker labels in the Dec 20, 2016 debate are inconsistent; the opposing Councillor Penner (label D) and the seconding Penner (label E) could not be told apart with certainty. Earl Funk later said (2018 financial plan hearing 0:24:42) he voted against the 2017 budget 'because of the massively inflated cost of the Performing Arts Centre' and the closed process.

title: Summer in the City governance board created
summary: At its Nov 2016 organizational meeting council created a governance board for the Summer in the City festival and ratified four of six community members.
status_detail: Board created and four members ratified; more appointments promised.
figures: Board of 6 members (mayor, 2016-11-01 organizational 0:08:23).

title: Steinbach wins urban beautification awards; council credits Parks and Rec staff
summary: Council received word that Steinbach won the Royal Oak and Shield for urban beautification (7,501+ category). Earl Funk's opening in April 2017 described the parks staff and work behind it.
status_detail: Award accepted by Mayor Goertzen and Councillor Fehr (Funk, 2017-04-18 opening).
figures: 11 full-time and 29 seasonal Parks and Rec staff (Funk, citing parks head, 2017-04-18 0:00:08).

title: Library, Arts Council and Mennonite Heritage Village funded as core grant groups; extra requests taken as information
summary: Under its grants policy council funded a small set of core organizations each year (Jake Epp Library, Steinbach Arts Council, Mennonite Heritage Village, Chamber of Commerce) and took most other requests, including additional Mennonite Heritage Village requests, as information.
status_detail: 2017 grants accepted Mar 20, 2018 (R18-065).
figures: 2017 grants: Jake Epp Library $327,315; Steinbach Arts Council $152,705; Mennonite Heritage Village $50,000; Southeastman Filipino Association $250 (minutes R18-065).
reasons: fairness-precedent: Focused grants policy for core groups; other requests reviewed at the fall grants session. (council (grants policy))

title: Accessible Parking By-law 2083: fine doubled to $100 and 'handicapped' wording replaced
summary: As part of the move to administrative penalties, council renamed its handicapped parking by-law the Accessible Parking By-law and raised the fine from $50 to $100.
status_detail: Third reading R17-147, Jul 18, 2017.
figures: Fine raised from $50 to $100 (City Manager, 2017-06-20 1:00:50).

title: Neighbourhood playground renewals funded with Community Places grants (Chote Park 2017, Giesbrecht Park 2018)
summary: Council kept renewing older neighbourhood playgrounds (Southwood, Poplar Park, Chote Park, Giesbrecht Park), applying each time for provincial Community Places grants; it also applied for $50,000 for Aquatic Centre repairs in 2018.
status_detail: Chote Park grant of up to $10,557 approved (Nov 21, 2017); Giesbrecht Park application approved R18-117 and grant acknowledged Aug 7, 2018.
figures: Chote Park grant up to $10,557 (Zwaagstra, 2017-11-21 0:32:59); Giesbrecht Park up to $12,000 (R18-117); Aquatic Centre up to $50,000 (R18-118).
mover: Earl Funk (Chote 2017, Giesbrecht 2018); Cari Penner (Aquatic Centre)

title: Fehr asks for a study of accessible parking stalls on Main Street
summary: Following a resident's letter, John Fehr moved that administration examine accessible parking spaces along Main Street. Michael Zwaagstra and one Councillor Penner argued it was not feasible or a good use of staff time; the mayor supported asking the question and the motion carried.
status_detail: No report back found in transcripts to Nov 2018.
reasons: study-first: Expected a report saying it is not feasible; accessible stalls belong in private lots near entrances. (Michael Zwaagstra)
public: Part of a resident's letter asked that an area on Main Street be used for accessible parking in winter.
vote: carried, divided (against: Zwaagstra; one Councillor Penner argued against)

title: Mayor asks about emerald ash borer threat; city had stopped planting ash about five years earlier
summary: After emerald ash borer was found in Winnipeg, Mayor Goertzen asked administration about a strategy for the city's thousands of ash trees. The City Manager said the city had stopped planting ash about five years earlier and expected a preservation program similar to the Dutch elm program.
status_detail: No ash-tree program came to council by Nov 2018 in the transcripts searched.
reasons: study-first: Province still evaluating best procedures; city in contact with provincial forestry branch. (Troy Warkentin (staff))

title: Pat Porter Active Living Centre asks for a grant in lieu of taxes; not included in the 2018 budget
summary: Serving Seniors Inc. asked council for a yearly grant in lieu of property taxes for the Pat Porter Active Living Centre, saying it had run deficits and that the grants policy favoured select groups. The 2018 financial plan made no change to grants; Earl Funk contrasted the seniors' treatment with the golf course land deal.
status_detail: No change to grants in the 2018 financial plan (Director of Finance, hearing 0:16:20); the mayor said the policy would be reviewed and the centre notified.
figures: Centre deficits totalling $38,572 over 3 years; property taxes $33,600 over the same years; 270 members; ~4,500 volunteer hours (delegation, 2018-02-20; minutes).
reasons: fairness-precedent: Council has a longstanding, focused grants policy. (Chris Goertzen)
public: Delegates D.E. and L.M. (Pat Porter Active Living Centre) said the policy 'shows favoritism' and asked for equitable funding for seniors.

title: Council asks Ottawa to remove the Canada Summer Jobs attestation
summary: Council unanimously asked the Prime Minister and Minister of Employment to remove the 2018 Canada Summer Jobs attestation, which required applicants to affirm respect for rights including reproductive rights and freedom from discrimination on grounds including sexual orientation and gender identity, in support of organizations that 'cannot in good conscience' check the box.
status_detail: R18-055 carried unanimously; Earl Funk asked on Mar 20, 2018 when the letter was mailed.
notes: Included because the attestation named sexual orientation and gender identity; council framed its objection as protecting faith-based and community organizations' freedom of conscience. Also covered in the advocacy topic.

title: Pathways: Park Hill connection funded; neighbours' request to remove Cottonwood pathway declined
summary: The 2018 budget put about $125,000 of new tax revenue toward a $250,000 pathway to the Park Hill subdivision. Separately, residents asked the city to remove a sidewalk on a public reserve off Cottonwood Bend because of student loitering and damage; administration and council declined, preferring RCMP monitoring, Citizens on Patrol and talks with the school division.
status_detail: Park Hill pathway in the adopted 2018 financial plan. Cottonwood pathway kept by consensus (Jul 17, 2018) with a letter to Hanover School Division and Citizens on Patrol involvement.
figures: Park Hill pathway $250,000, about $125,000 from new tax revenue (Siemens, 2018 financial plan hearing 0:18:11); about a dozen incidents over 5 years at Cottonwood (City Manager, 2018-07-17 1:48:48).
reasons: already-doing-enough: Removing the sidewalk would not help and the city wants more sidewalks. (Michael Zwaagstra)
public: Residents P.F. and M.F. and a July 10, 2018 petition asked that the Cottonwood sidewalk be removed or closed.
vote: financial plan 4-3 (against: Zwaagstra, S. Penner, Funk, over the golf course land deal); Cottonwood by consensus

title: $65,000 match for Steinbach Arts Centre building repairs: tabled 4-3 in June, approved unanimously in September 2018
summary: Susan Penner moved that the city match the Arts Council's $65,000 Clearview Co-op Community Spaces grant from the Recreation and Culture reserve to repair the city-owned arts centre. In June a majority tabled it, wanting a plan and grants-policy clarity; after an Arts Council presentation in September it passed unanimously.
status_detail: R18-205 carried unanimously Sept 4, 2018; June 19 motion tabled 4-3 (R18-148).
figures: $65,000 city match from the Recreation and Culture reserve fund (R18-205); total project about $180,000–$190,000 including $20,000 private and $25,000 in-kind (Arts Council, 2018-09-04 0:32:04); building 84 years old (June motion, minutes).
reasons: fairness-precedent: An ad hoc grant outside the grants policy sets a precedent; fix the policy first. (Michael Zwaagstra); study-first: Wanted a concrete plan rather than a reactionary grant. (John Fehr); study-first: Wanted more information from administration. (Jac Siemens)
public: The Steinbach Arts Council (delegates A.B. and C.R.P.) presented its renovation plan; it was one of 24 of 792 applicants chosen for the Co-op grant.
vote: June: tabled 4-3 (for tabling: Siemens, Zwaagstra, Fehr, Goertzen; against: S. Penner, C. Penner, Funk). Sept: unanimous

title: 2018 Official Community Plan update: resident flags a lack of designated park space
summary: At the July 2018 hearing on the new Official Community Plan (Bylaw 2099) and zoning by-law, resident T.B. said the map showed a large void of park and green-space designation south of Loewen Boulevard and east of Giesbrecht, and asked what 'inclusive community' meant. Council gave the plan second reading.
status_detail: Plan given second reading and sent to the minister; no change addressing the green-space point was found in the transcript.
public: T.B. (resident) asked that the plan be left to the new council and that parks and green space be designated downtown.
notes: Council's response to the green-space comment was not located in the portions read.

title: Council signs the provincial Community Forest grant agreement for Dutch elm work
summary: Council entered into Manitoba's Community Forest Grant Agreement #6076, which replaced the long-running Dutch Elm Disease Control Program and gives partial funding for pruning and treating the city's elm trees.
status_detail: Agreement approved unanimously (R18-277).
figures: Grant amount not stated at the meeting; Siemens said the province had 'reduced the funding' (transcript 0:37:40).
decision_source: minutes (mover/seconder from transcript; minutes text extract omits them)
notes: Seconder heard as 'Councillor Penner'; which Penner is not clear.

title: Proclamation requests (Agape House, Canadian Blood Services) received as information
summary: Agape House asked council to support a proclamation in December 2018 (for December 6) and again in November 2019; Canadian Blood Services asked in May 2019 for a proclamation for World Blood Donor Day and National Blood Donor Week. Each was received as information; no proclamation was issued on the record.
status_detail: Received as information (minutes 2018-12-04 item 29; 2019-11-19 item 18; 2019-05-07 delegation). No proclamation recorded.
public: A Canadian Blood Services representative (S.R.) presented as a delegation on May 7, 2019.
notes: The Dec 6 date suggests the National Day of Remembrance and Action on Violence Against Women; the letter itself was not read on the record.

title: Park reserve land closed, swapped or sold for development
summary: Council closed or reconfigured public reserve (park) land several times: Harmony Lane (2018, after the developer settled with an objector), relocating Parks and Recreation zoning to a detention pond area (By-law 2126, 2019), Park Hill reserve with Bush Farm Road widening (By-law 2181, 2021), removal of a reserve in a 2022 subdivision, and a sale of reserve land to Priority Auto. All votes were unanimous.
figures: Reserve parcel sold to Priority Auto for $19,000 (R22-225).
reasons: already-doing-enough: reconfiguration lets development proceed; developer resolved the objector's concern (Michael Zwaagstra)
public: An objector at the Harmony Lane hearing (2018) withdrew after the developer offered an easement.
mover: Michael Zwaagstra; Michael Zwaagstra; Jake Hiebert; Susan Penner
seconder: Susan Penner; Jake Hiebert; Damian Penner; Bill Hiebert
notes: Net change in park acreage not stated on the record.

title: Annual grants to the library, Arts Council and Mennonite Heritage Village
summary: Each year council accepted its grant summary, which included the Jake Epp Library (the largest grant), the Steinbach Arts Council and Mennonite Heritage Village. Separate grant requests from Mennonite Heritage Village (Dec 2018, Dec 2020) were received as information for budget deliberations.
status_detail: Grant summaries accepted unanimously: R19-073 (2018), R20-064 (2019), R22-066 (2020 and 2021).
figures: Library $327,315 (2018), $342,983.74 (2019), $336,680 (2020 and 2021); Arts Council $152,705 (2018), $155,400 (2019); Mennonite Heritage Village $50,000 (2018), $53,200 (2019), $52,500 (2021) - minutes grant summaries. Library support 'just over $400,000' in the 2020 and 2021 budgets (budget hearings).
mover: Bill Hiebert; Michael Zwaagstra; Damian Penner
seconder: Susan Penner; Jake Hiebert; Michael Zwaagstra
notes: The 2020/2021 Arts Council figure is garbled in the minutes text extract and is not given.

title: Council twice refuses to waive the street-edge tree and shrub requirement
summary: In January 2019 (an apartment at 29 Cambridge Way) and October 2020 (a truck business at 435 PTH 12 North) builders asked to skip the zoning by-law's street-edge landscaping. Both times a majority denied the variance, saying the 2010 tree-and-shrub rule is good policy and exceptions would set a precedent; Siemens and Susan Penner voted to grant both.
status_detail: V-2019-01 denied 5-2 (R19-003 defeated, R19-004 carried); V-2020-24 denied 4-3 (R20-197 defeated, R20-198 carried).
figures: By-law 2100 requires one tree per 30 ft and three shrubs per 20 ft of street frontage (City Manager, 2020-10-20 0:30:06).
reasons: fairness-precedent: an after-the-fact exception would invite 'build first, ask forgiveness' (Michael Zwaagstra); fairness-precedent: argued for the waivers: trees would not survive in asphalt, and the area has reduced city services (Jac Siemens)
public: The 2019 applicants (M.U. and J.U.) said the omission was an honest oversight and offered to plant elsewhere on the site; no one objected at either hearing.
vote: 5-2 (against: S. Penner, J. Siemens); 4-3 (against: J. Siemens, S. Penner, B. Hiebert)
notes: Applicant names are in the minutes; shown by initials here.

title: Request for a lift at the outdoor pool and hot tub referred to staff
summary: A resident (C.K.B.) wrote that the indoor pools have a lift but the outdoor pool and hot tub do not, citing her daughter with cerebral palsy. Councillor Zwaagstra called accessibility important and council agreed by consensus to have administration report back.
status_detail: Consensus for administration to review and report (minutes 2019-02-19 item 13.1). No report back on a lift was found in later transcripts or minutes; the 2020 renovation covered lighting, acoustic panels and painting.
reasons: study-first: refer to staff for options and recommendations as pool upgrades proceed (Michael Zwaagstra)
public: C.K.B. (letter) asked for lift access to the outdoor pool and hot tub.
notes: Follow-through unverified; Strategic Priorities Committee meetings are not recorded.

title: One-time $7,527 technology grant to the Jake Epp Library
summary: Councillor Damian Penner, council's library board representative, brought a motion for a one-time grant to replace the library's failing computers and server. Council approved it unanimously, the mayor cautioning that it was a special one-time need on top of the regular grant.
status_detail: R19-076 carried unanimously.
figures: $7,527.20 one-time (R19-076); library budgets $2,000/yr for technology (transcript 0:56:36); city grant to the library $327,315 in 2018 (R19-073).

title: Resident's proposal for a new city flag received as information
summary: A resident (W.T.) sent council a letter and drawing proposing a city flag. The mayor asked whether to take it as information and council agreed, with no discussion.
status_detail: Received as information (minutes 2019-04-02 item 21). No further action found.
public: W.T. proposed a city flag design (letter on agenda page 87).

title: Aquatic Centre renovation moved up to 2020 while COVID-19 closed the pool
summary: Council funded a study of the 18-year-old Aquatic Centre (2019) and applied for federal-provincial money for a $2.735M renewal. When COVID-19 closed the pool in March 2020, council had the planned 2021 lighting, acoustic and painting work tendered and done in summer 2020 so the pool would not close again later.
status_detail: Study grant application R19-123; ICIP application R19-197; tender awarded R20-118 to Ernst Hansch Construction, paid from the Recreation Reserve. Reopening projected for Sept 14, 2020 (transcript 0:21:44).
notes: Whether the 2019 lift request was included is not stated.

title: Southeast Event Centre partnership: 'recreation and cultural facility renewal' made a priority
summary: Council signed a memorandum of understanding with Southeast Event Centre Inc., a private community group, to build a downtown event centre replacing the 1967 Centennial Arena, and applied for federal-provincial funding. Borrowing and design followed in 2021-2022. (Covered in detail in other reports.)
status_detail: MOU R19-193 and grant application R19-198 (2019); design contract R21-199 (2021); local improvement by-law 2186 third reading R22-100 (2022). All unanimous.
figures: Project cost $42.5M, $17.5M requested from ICIP (transcript 1:03:19; R19-198 $42,491,093); 2,500 seats; borrowing $7.5M (2022-04-19 0:13:45); design contract $1,898,430 (R21-199).
public: Southeast Event Centre Inc. presented the concept on Oct 1, 2019.
notes: Arts/performing-arts venue was not part of this project; Bill Hiebert said voters had asked about a performing arts centre or multiplex (0:43:50, speaker identification medium, not quoted).

title: Clearspring Greens pathway: from an 80/20 resident levy to a 50/50 plan after 78 objections
summary: Residents of the rural-residential Clearspring Greens area had long asked for a safe walking link to the city. In January 2020 council approved an asphalt, lit pathway with most of the cost levied on 146 lots; Siemens and Jake Hiebert wanted a cheaper limestone path. After 78 objections went to the Municipal Board, Susan Penner had the plan cancelled in January 2021 and replaced with a 50/50 split capped at $1,610 per lot and no lighting. The path was built in 2021.
status_detail: By-law 2132 first/second reading 5-2 (R20-004/R20-005); lighting moved to city reserve 6-1 (R20-012); plan cancelled and redone (R21-011/R21-012); By-law 2168 passed (R21-076) and tender awarded (R21-077); debenture By-law 2195 (R22-046). Councillors cited the finished path in Oct 2021.
figures: Original estimate $625,000, $4,280.82 per lot up front or $1,044.05/yr for 5 years (minutes 2020-01-07); about $2,850 per lot after lighting was removed (2021-01-05 0:34:03); new cap $1,610 per lot (R21-012); budget about $650,000 (2021-04-20 0:21:57).
reasons: fairness-precedent: the neighbourhood that asked for it should pay most; not fair to raise other taxpayers' share (Michael Zwaagstra); cost: a connecting path that mainly benefits the homes paying for it (Damian Penner)
public: Many residents objected at the Jan 7, 2020 hearing to the cost (about $4,280 per lot), the route and the lighting, while others stressed children's safety walking on Park Road; 78 objections were filed with the Municipal Board.
vote: 5-2 (against: J. Siemens, J. Hiebert) in 2020; unanimous in 2021
notes: Also covered in neighbourhood-services reporting. Resident objectors are named in the minutes; not named here.

title: Barrier-Free Manitoba's request for support received as information
summary: Barrier-Free Manitoba asked for a letter supporting its Canadian Accessibility Standards Development (CASDO) grant application. Council took it as information without discussion.
status_detail: Received as information (minutes 2020-03-17). No letter of support recorded.
notes: The meeting was shortened for COVID-19 distancing.

title: Council presses the library board to reopen after COVID-19 closures
summary: In May 2020 library board representative Damian Penner reported on the library's phased reopening (pre-ordered pick-up). The mayor passed on families' calls for it to reopen, and Zwaagstra asked why curbside service had not been offered since March and when people could go in and choose books.
status_detail: Phase 1 pick-up began mid-May 2020; the next phase was 'to be determined' (transcript 1:08:31). By Nov 2020 curbside pickup continued under restrictions (2020-11-17 1:20:24).
public: Families phoned the mayor asking for the library to reopen (as reported by the mayor).

title: Filipino community presents Manitoba's Filipino Heritage Month resolution to council
summary: K.O., past president of the South Eastman Filipino association, presented council with a copy of the provincial resolution designating June as Filipino Heritage Month and spoke of drawing strength from cultural diversity amid racial tensions. The mayor and Councillor Zwaagstra praised the Filipino community as an integral part of Steinbach.
status_detail: Received with thanks (minutes 8.1). No city proclamation was requested or made.
public: K.O.: the pandemic, economic uncertainty and 'racial tensions' call for 'more compassion, tolerance, and justice'.

title: Councillor Bill Hiebert speaks on racism after George Floyd's death
summary: In his June 16, 2020 opening remarks Bill Hiebert called the killing of George Floyd an injustice, noted Steinbach now has over 55 ethnic groups, publicly apologized for attitudes he had to change, and urged everyone to accept all people as equals; he also praised the local RCMP. No motion or policy followed.
status_detail: Statement only; no council motion, policy or program on racism appears in Nov 2018 - Oct 2022.
figures: Over 55 ethnic groups; 55 flags in the 2019 parade (per Southeast immigrant services, transcript 0:00:15).

title: First city dog park approved and built at L.A. Barkman Park
summary: After years of requests, the city applied for and council approved a conditional use for a dog park in the northwest corner of L.A. Barkman Park, funded in the 2021 capital budget along with a basketball court. Council members cited it as built by October 2021.
status_detail: CU-2021-01 approved unanimously (R21-052); included in the 2021 financial plan; mentioned as completed in Oct 2021 opening remarks.
figures: Cost not stated on the record.
public: No objections at the hearing; members said residents had asked for years.

title: Street racing and noise on Main Street: council asks for a traffic officer and red-light cameras
summary: After letters and calls from residents about street racing on Main Street, council asked for an 18th RCMP officer dedicated to traffic and for provincial authority to install red-light cameras. The traffic officer started in May 2022, and the mayor reported less engine revving downtown.
status_detail: R21-195 carried unanimously. The traffic officer started in May 2022 (2022-05-17 0:18:40). No provincial approval of red-light cameras was found in the period.
figures: Extra officer about $200,000/yr (2021-09-07 1:05:57, speaker not identified); 17 officers in 2021, 18 in 2022.
reasons: enforcement-limits: existing officers are pulled to emergencies and cannot sit on Main Street (Michael Zwaagstra); provincial-responsibility: red-light cameras need provincial permission (Earl Funk)
public: Letters from residents B.U., S.M. and L.D. about street racing; the mayor said he had been 'bombarded' with emails, calls and store visits.
notes: Overlaps with the crime-policing topic. The noise by-law itself was not discussed.

title: City recognizes the National Day for Truth and Reconciliation
summary: Following the federal and provincial governments, council resolved to recognize September 30 as a day of observance on the impacts of residential schools, close city offices and half-mast flags on city buildings. Zwaagstra cited TRC Call to Action 80; Susan Penner spoke of generational trauma; the mayor spoke of healing.
status_detail: R21-207 carried unanimously.
reasons: neutral-policy: appropriate because senior governments recognized the day and the city is also a level of government (Michael Zwaagstra)
notes: No land acknowledgement or further reconciliation item found in the period.

title: Councillor Siemens on the meaning of City Hall's large Canadian flag
summary: In opening remarks Jac Siemens told the history of the 80-foot pole and 15-by-30-foot Canadian flag raised in 1992 for Canada's 125th, noting the city flies 45 Canadian flags and calling the flag a reminder of national pride.
status_detail: Statement only; council had no written flag policy in the period.
figures: Pole 80 ft, flag 15x30 ft, $1,300 per flag replaced yearly; 45 Canadian flags flown (transcript 0:00:18).

title: Council passes a resolution of support for the people of Ukraine
summary: After Russia's invasion, the mayor described the situation in Zaporizhzhia, Steinbach's sister city, and asked council to show support. Zwaagstra moved a resolution of support; members spoke of family ties through Steinbach's Mennonite settlers.
status_detail: R22-058 carried unanimously.
notes: The existing report links the motion text at 1:08:31 (word-level time); the turn starts at 1:08:24.

title: Request to fly the Ukrainian flag at City Hall received as information
summary: Choice Dental Care asked the city to raise the Ukrainian flag. The mayor said he preferred practical help, describing work with Eastman Immigrant Services, the MP's office and churches to host Ukrainian families, and said 'This is our Canadian flag.' Zwaagstra agreed and the request was taken as information.
status_detail: Received as information (minutes 2022-03-15); the flag was not raised. The mayor and Councillor Siemens later took part in Chamber-run bus tours for Ukrainian newcomers (June 2022, per the Chamber on 2022-10-18).
reasons: neutral-policy: 'we're Canadians. This is our Canadian flag'; prefers working to bring people over (Earl Funk); community-led: churches, immigrant services and employers are hosting and sponsoring families (Earl Funk)
public: A business (Choice Dental Care) made the request; the mayor mentioned a petition and supporting letters received.
notes: The existing report cites 0:45:45 (word-level time); the turn starts at 0:41:14. No written flag policy existed. Outside council, residents raised their own Pride flags at City Hall in Aug 2022 after organizers said the city refused (CBC, https://www.cbc.ca/lite/story/1.6551138); no Pride flag request appears in the council record for this period.

title: Non-resident library fees and the idea of a regional library
summary: Susan Penner asked about the Jake Epp Library's non-resident fee; Damian Penner explained that about one in six patrons live outside Steinbach and pay a fee, and that a regional library would need neighbouring municipalities to join. Council took it as information.
status_detail: Received as information; no regionalization step in the period (talks ended in Jan 2026 per the 2022-2026 report).
figures: Non-resident membership about $110 (transcript 0:19:01).
reasons: community-led: residents of other municipalities should press their own councils to join (Damian Penner)

title: Council asks the province for no-engine-brake signs on all four highways
summary: Bill Hiebert raised residents' complaints about truck engine-brake noise early and late. Council resolved to ask Manitoba Transportation and Infrastructure for signs on PTH 12 North and South and PTH 52 East and West; Siemens added all four highways.
status_detail: R22-177 carried unanimously; no provincial reply on the record.
reasons: provincial-responsibility: signs on provincial highways need Manitoba Infrastructure approval and a council resolution (Adam Thiessen (staff))
public: Residents south of Steinbach complained to Bill Hiebert about engine-brake noise.
notes: The existing report links Hiebert at 0:18:29 (word-level); the turn starts at 0:18:26.

title: Council supports the Steinbach Arts Centre's provincial grant application
summary: Council passed a resolution supporting the Steinbach Arts Centre's application to Manitoba's Arts, Culture and Sport in Community Fund to improve its building and expand programs; it did the same for the Steinbach Skimmers swim club's starting blocks.
status_detail: R22-243 (Arts Centre) and R22-232 (Skimmers, $25,000) carried unanimously. Grant outcomes not on the record.
figures: Skimmers request $25,000 for 6 starting blocks (R22-232). Arts Centre amount not stated.

title: Chamber reports on Eastman Immigrant Services and Ukrainian newcomer tours
summary: The Steinbach Chamber of Commerce chair (C.B.) reported that newcomers continue to use its Eastman Immigrant Services, with 10-15 languages in the office, and that the mayor and Councillor Siemens joined June 2022 bus tours connecting Ukrainian newcomers with employers. Newcomer settlement in this period ran through the Chamber, not a city program.
status_detail: Delegation received (minutes 2022-10-18 item 10).
figures: Chamber and EIS staff 'up to 20' (transcript 0:43:44); 10-15 languages (minutes).
reasons: community-led: settlement services delivered by the Chamber with federal funding (Steinbach Chamber of Commerce)
public: C.B. (Chamber chair) presented.

title: Southeast Event Centre funded and built (covered in its own reports)
summary: Council added $11.4M in city funds and awarded the Event Centre (Nov 2022), then approved $8.5M more (Dec 2023). Members presented it as a quality-of-life and gathering space.
status_detail: Built and opened 2025; deadline extensions under the federal culture/recreation stream (R25-006, R25-215).
figures: $11.4M added (R22-255); $8.5M additional (R23-252).
notes: Detail belongs to the event centre/taxes topics.

title: Public reserve south of Acres Drive closed and sold to a neighbouring business
summary: Council closed a small city public reserve so most of it could be sold to the adjoining business to expand. No one objected at the hearing.
reasons: already-doing-enough: Small parcel; selling it lets a local business expand. (Michael Zwaagstra)

title: Steinbach Arts Council thanks city for a grant increase
summary: The city's grant to the Steinbach Arts Council was $166,317 in 2022. In September 2025 the Arts Council wrote to thank council for an increase; the mayor praised its growth past $1 million a year in revenue. The increase was decided in budget deliberations, not at a recorded council debate.
status_detail: Increase approved; per news reports (existing report) the operating top-up ($55,000 to $85,000) was for one year, with permanence to be decided around Nov 2026. No performance-venue plan came to council.
figures: 2022 grant $166,317.26 (R23-039); 2026 grant $185,400 per existing report (SteinbachOnline), not verified in minutes.
reasons: community-led: Mayor has suggested a community/donor group lead any theatre planning (news, per existing report). (Mayor Earl Funk)
notes: Grant decision made in unrecorded budget sessions; amounts after 2022 not confirmed from minutes.

title: Festivals run by volunteers; Summer in the City's 2027 funding request deferred to budget
summary: Councillors praised volunteer-run festivals (Summer in the City, Pioneer Days at Mennonite Heritage Village). A provincial $5,000 Canada Day grant was received in 2023. Summer in the City's request for 2027 funding was taken as information in July 2026 to be dealt with in November budget talks.
status_detail: 2027 Summer in the City request pending in budget deliberations (Nov 2026).
figures: $5,000 provincial Canada Day grant (May 16, 2023 minutes).
reasons: community-led: Festivals depend on volunteer organizations. (Damian Penner)

title: Library support rises; non-resident fees raised; security cameras for the library left undecided
summary: City support for the Jake Epp Library grew from about $454,000 (2023 budget) to $515,000 (2026). In 2025 the library board, at council's request, raised non-resident fees from $110 to $165. In July 2026 Councillors Siemens and Zwaagstra asked why the library, which had raised security concerns twice, was left off a $200,000 provincial security grant list; the decision was postponed.
status_detail: Funding increased in 2025-2026 budgets; fees raised July 2025; library cameras not decided on the record by Nov 2026.
figures: Library support $454,000 (2023), $453,000 (2024), $455,000 (2025), $515,000 (2026) per financial plan presentations; non-resident fee $110 -> $165 (Siemens, May 6, 2025).
reasons: cost: Not enough grant money for every site; council could choose to prioritize the library. (Adam Thiessen (staff))
notes: Library board appointments (routine) were ratified throughout the term (e.g., R23-120, R24-058, R24-069, R24-132, R25-237).

title: Budgets keep recreation as a priority alongside infrastructure, without a recreation master plan
summary: In financial plan debates members described recreation and 260 acres of green space as quality-of-life pieces and refused to cut them, while saying infrastructure comes first. No recreation and culture master plan came to council.
status_detail: Recreation budgets maintained and grown each year; no master plan adopted.
figures: Recreation services ~ a third of operating budget: $10.7M (2023), $11.2M (2024), $12.8M (2026) per financial plan presentations; 260 acres of green space (Siemens, Mar 21, 2023).
reasons: cost: Infrastructure is what council should be doing despite pressure for other projects. (Susan Penner)

title: Tree-planting grants won for the Event Centre and Soccer Park; Dutch elm funding received
summary: The city signed a Tree Canada community tree grant MOU (Aug 2024), applied to FCM's Green Municipal Fund (Dec 2024), and won FCM grants of $46,170 for tree canopy at the Southeast Event Centre (July 2025) and $67,160 for tree planting at the Soccer Park (Apr 2026). Provincial Dutch elm disease funding letters were received in 2023 and 2025.
status_detail: Grants received as information; plantings tied to the Event Centre east parking lot (2025) and the Soccer Park.
figures: $46,170 (FCM, July 2, 2025 minutes); $67,160 (FCM, Apr 21, 2026 minutes).
notes: R24-242 text is an FCM Green Municipal Fund application resolution; its project scope was not confirmed beyond the minutes excerpt.

title: Main Street racing and engine noise handled through RCMP traffic enforcement
summary: Racing, revving and loud vehicles on Main Street were raised at every annual RCMP report. Council set traffic enforcement as a policing priority (May 2023), credited its dedicated municipal traffic officer for fewer complaints (Apr 2024), agreed by consensus to joint RCMP-Ste. Anne enforcement when reports rose again (May 2025), and welcomed a Main Street blitz (Sept 2026). The noise by-law itself was not reviewed.
status_detail: Enforcement continued (dedicated traffic officer, joint patrols, Sept 2026 blitz); racing complaints recurred in 2025 and 2026. No change to the 2003 noise by-law came to council.
figures: RCMP often 2-4 officers short of the requested complement (Zwaagstra, May 6, 2025 transcript).
reasons: enforcement-limits: RCMP detachment is often several officers short, limiting enforcement. (Michael Zwaagstra); not-council-role: Enforcement is an RCMP matter; council sets priorities and supports extra patrols. (Mayor Earl Funk)
public: Residents' complaints about racing were reported second-hand by councillors (Zwaagstra, Siemens/Hiebert in Sept 2026).
vote: consensus (May 2, 2023 priorities approved by resolution; May 6, 2025 joint-enforcement consensus)
notes: 2026-09-15 questions on racing came from speakers the map marks low/medium confidence, so they are not quoted. Steinbach's Noise Control By-law 1662 (2003) has no decibel limits or fine schedule (existing report; city website).

title: Councillors state City Hall should not fly cause flags, issue proclamations or use DEI criteria
summary: In opening remarks, Councillor Zwaagstra repeatedly praised council for not issuing proclamations, raising multiple flags or making climate declarations, and criticised DEI criteria; Councillor Damian Penner criticised DEI hiring and quick labels of 'homophobic' or 'racist'. No flag, proclamation, Pride or anti-racism item came to a council vote in Nov 2022 - Nov 2026, and the city has no written flag or proclamation policy.
status_detail: No request, policy or motion on flags, proclamations, Pride or anti-racism appears in the minutes for the period; the stance is stated by individual members, not adopted as policy.
reasons: neutral-policy: City should focus on core services rather than symbolic flags, proclamations or declarations. (Michael Zwaagstra); neutral-policy: DEI hiring leads to groupthink; debate is too readily labelled hateful. (Damian Penner)
public: Outside council (news, unverified on the council record): residents put up their own Pride flagpoles at City Hall in 2022; Pride march threats in 2025; council members invited to the 2026 march did not attend (existing report, SteinbachOnline/CBC).
notes: Pride/flag events in 2022 predate this period; they are described from news only.

title: Council backs Skimmers and Curling Club bids to the provincial Arts, Culture and Sport fund
summary: Council passed support resolutions for the Steinbach Skimmers ($25,000) and Steinbach Curling Club ($17,242) applications to Manitoba's Arts, Culture and Sport in Community Fund.
status_detail: R23-087 and R23-088 carried.

title: City resumes weed control after province loosens cosmetic pesticide ban
summary: Councillor Zwaagstra noted council's long lobbying to lift the provincial cosmetic pesticide ban; the city manager confirmed the city had resumed its pre-2015 weed control program within provincial limits.
status_detail: Weed control resumed in permitted areas (city manager).
reasons: provincial-responsibility: Pesticide rules are set by the province; council lobbied for change. (Michael Zwaagstra)

title: Newcomer services left to the Chamber and Steinbach Economic Development; city declines to fund the immigration pilot and ends SED grant
summary: The Chamber reported growth of its Eastman Immigrant Services (2023) and Steinbach Economic Development (SED) described work with the province and Ottawa to attract and keep newcomers (2024). In March 2025 SED said it would run the federal Rural Community Immigration Pilot (RCIP) from its own reserves; councillors questioned the lack of consultation and the mayor warned pilots get downloaded to cities. In August 2025 council voted not to renew its five-year matching grant to SED after Dec 31, 2025 (R25-158); Councillor Siemens, who moved it, said the city had put in $65,000 a year since 2021. The mayor's 2026 State of the City cited immigrants as about 28% of the workforce.
status_detail: R25-158 (Aug 5, 2025): city does not renew SED grant after Dec 31, 2025. No city-run newcomer or welcoming program was proposed.
figures: $65,000/year city grant to SED, 2021-2025 (Siemens, Aug 5, 2025 transcript); RCIP run without federal money (minutes Mar 18, 2025).
reasons: provincial-responsibility: Federal/provincial pilots without funding tend to be downloaded to municipalities. (Mayor Earl Funk); cost: Said the office had not produced the development council hoped for, after the city put in $65,000 a year since 2021 (his figure). (Jac Siemens); community-led: Economic development/attraction best left to the Chamber, landowners and business owners. (Jac Siemens)
public: C.B. (Chamber president) and M.B. (SED director) presented; SED said RCIP fills workforce shortages and helps existing newcomers stay.
notes: Eastman Immigrant Services federal funding (about $2.6M 2025-28) is from the existing report's external source, not re-verified here.

title: Banman Heritage Foundation presents a Town Square statue honouring Russlaender and later newcomers
summary: A private heritage foundation presented a 9-foot bronze statue for the Town Square by the Millennium Clock Tower, marking 100 years since the Russlaender Mennonite migration and paying tribute to all who fled their homelands, including recent Ukrainian arrivals. The mayor welcomed it as public art; council received it as information.
status_detail: Received as information with the mayor's support; privately led. Installation is not recorded in later council meetings.
figures: Bronze, 9 ft, about 1,800 lb (delegation, transcript).
public: D.B. (Banman Heritage Foundation) presented.
notes: Whether the statue was installed was not checked outside council records.

title: Hampton Village green space named Chris Goertzen Park
summary: Continuing the custom of naming a park for each former mayor, council named the Hampton Village green space, where neighbours had added a play structure, garden and picnic shelter, after former Mayor Chris Goertzen.
status_detail: R23-183 (repeated as R23-193 on Sept 19, 2023).

title: New public reserve created near Main Street for a future creek-bed pathway
summary: Council created a public reserve from city land plus a newly acquired parcel near Main Street, protecting a water line and the old Steinbach Creek bed for a possible future pedestrian corridor.
notes: Street name in the transcript is 'Goosen Avenue'.

title: Part of a Wyndham Estate Drive park reserve closed so a developer could add a lot, over a resident's objection
summary: Stonebridge Development asked to close part of public reserve it had dedicated in Hampton Village to create one more residential lot. A neighbour objected that it benefited the developer; councillors said the area still had more green space than required and room for a future active transportation route.
reasons: already-doing-enough: Green space still exceeds by-law requirements; one more lot adds housing. (Michael Zwaagstra)
public: D.M. (resident) objected: benefits the developer, not residents; traffic on the single access.

title: Public reserve converted to road to extend Heritage Parkway for the Steinbach Campus Foundation
summary: Council closed part of a public reserve north of Loewen Boulevard so Heritage Parkway could be extended for institutional development by the Steinbach Campus Foundation. No objections.

title: Truck yard next to Creekside homes denied after neighbours cite noise, lights and safety
summary: A conditional use for a trucking yard at 45 Tower Avenue drew objections from neighbours about noise, lights, dust, water wells and children's safety on the walking path. Council unanimously denied it.
status_detail: Conditional Use CU-2023-02 denied (R24-009), as residents asked.
figures: Applicant: 19 trucks, about 60 could park on 4 acres (minutes).
public: Several neighbours objected (G.P., J.L., S.U., D.M., C.W., K.D., H.W.): noise, lighting, dust, wells, traffic, child safety; C.W. said the existing steel plant is already loud.

title: Members speak about belonging and newcomer communities in openings and event reports
summary: Council members reported on newcomer community events (the mayor at a Filipino-owned business reopening, Councillor Jake Hiebert at the first Sikh celebration, at the mayor's request) and gave openings on loneliness and community connection (Susan Penner) and Canada as a 'cultural mosaic' united by shared values (Damian Penner). These were remarks, not policy.
status_detail: Members attended and welcomed newcomer community events; no welcoming, multicultural or inclusion policy or program was brought to council. The city's Community Safety and Well-Being Plan (posted Mar 2026) names belonging and inclusion as a priority, but council did not discuss its actions on the record.
reasons: community-led: Loneliness is not a municipal responsibility; city provides spaces, residents build connection. (Susan Penner)
notes: CSWB plan content (belonging/inclusion priority, timelines TBD) is from the plan document per the existing report, not from council discussion.

title: Park Hill and Kootenay Way park reserves closed and re-opened in new locations
summary: Twice, at the developer's request, council closed public reserves in the Park Hill development so they could be realigned with new subdivision phases; staff said no reserve area would be lost.

title: Regional library explored, then dropped to keep the Jake Epp Library's autonomy
summary: Council supported a southeastern Manitoba regional library in principle and joined the provincial working group (Nov 2024), with Councillors Siemens and Bill Hiebert as members. After most municipalities withdrew and under the 2023 provincial funding formula, council ended its participation in January 2026 and kept the current library governance, leaving the door open for later.
status_detail: R26-009: city ends the regionalization process as proposed; Jake Epp Library continues with current governance.
reasons: provincial-responsibility: Province's 2023 funding formula makes regionalization unworkable; most municipalities said no. (Michael Zwaagstra); cost: Funding formula changed in 2023; not enough partners (speaker merged, medium). (Bill Hiebert); fairness-precedent: Library must not lose its autonomy; funding and governance model unclear. (Mayor Earl Funk)

title: Dog park rules made enforceable in new Animal Control By-law
summary: A rewritten Animal Control By-law put the Ellie Barkman Park dog park rules into law so officers can enforce them, raised fines and folded in the pit bull ban.

title: New Official Community Plan and Zoning By-law add park, green-space and accessibility policies
summary: The OCP/zoning review (begun 2023) added policies for park planning including universal accessibility for all ages and abilities, plus active transportation. The OCP was adopted in September 2025 and the Zoning By-law in January 2026, both unanimously.
status_detail: OCP By-law 2244 third reading Sept 16, 2025 (R25-184); Zoning By-law 2245 third reading Jan 20, 2026 (R26-015). No parks master plan followed in the period.
figures: Zoning by-law cut from 155 to 106 pages (D. Penner, Dec 3, 2024 transcript).

title: New zoning by-law makes emergency shelters and group homes conditional uses; discrimination concern raised
summary: At the April 2025 hearing on the new Zoning By-law, a councillor asked how conditional-use hearings protect against discrimination, and a resident (L.C.) raised the same concern. The mayor said conditional use lets council hear everyone and decide fairly. The by-law passed first and second readings that night and third reading in January 2026.
status_detail: Zoning By-law 2245 adopted (R25-071/072 Apr 1, 2025; R26-015 Jan 20, 2026) with shelters as conditional uses.
reasons: fairness-precedent: Public hearings let all sides be heard; objections do not decide the vote. (Mayor Earl Funk)
public: L.C. (resident) worried conditional-use hearings could allow discrimination against groups needing homes; other speakers opposed shelters or regulation generally.
notes: Covered more fully in the homelessness report.

title: First Active Transportation Plan accepted as a guide; projects unfunded
summary: Council accepted the city's first Active Transportation Plan (Urban Systems), which maps future pathways. Members called it a starting point; Councillor Zwaagstra warned the roughly $11 million of projects would not happen soon.
status_detail: Plan accepted (R25-096) as a guide; individual projects depend on future budgets and grants (e.g., 60% federal AT fund).
figures: About $11M total project cost (Zwaagstra, transcript).
reasons: cost: Price tags are high; much is far in the future. (Michael Zwaagstra)
public: Plan included a pop-up engagement at Summer in the City and an online survey (consultant).

title: Football club asks city for about $70,000 toward A.D. Penner Park floodlights
summary: The Eastman Raiders asked the city to fund about a third of field floodlights at A.D. Penner Park, with the club covering about $141,000. Councillors asked about cost overruns and grants; the mayor noted the budget is fixed once set.
status_detail: Received as a delegation; no funding decision found in council minutes.
figures: Club ~$141,000; city ask ~$70,000 (delegation, transcript).
reasons: cost: Budget is fixed once set; requests must fit the budget cycle. (Mayor Earl Funk)
public: M.B. and G.D. (Eastman Raiders) presented.

title: Outdoor pool renewal: two provincial grant applications, no funding yet
summary: Council applied to Manitoba's GROW program for the long-delayed outdoor pool deck and equipment renewal in Sept 2025 ($3.6M) and again in Oct 2026 ($3.85M, seeking $1.925M), saying the nearly 50-year-old pool is well used and costs rise if repairs wait.
status_detail: Applications submitted (R25-182; Oct 20, 2026 resolution); no grant decision on the record.
figures: $3.6M est. (Warkentin, Sept 16, 2025); $3.85M, 50% = $1.925M (city manager, Oct 20, 2026).
reasons: cost: Hard to find funding sources that fit recreation projects. (Troy Warkentin (City Manager))

title: Sports Heritage Committee extended with a $15,000 grant
summary: Council extended the Steinbach Sports Heritage Committee to 2027 and granted $15,000 for displaying sports history and memorabilia.
status_detail: R25-236, subject to the 2026 budget.

title: Seniors' apartment approved on Friesen Avenue land neighbours used as green space
summary: Steinbach Housing proposed a seniors' building at 185 Friesen Avenue. Neighbours said they were drawn by green space set aside in 1989 and objected to height and loss of green space. After an adjournment in March, council approved the use unanimously and the height/parking variance 5-2 in June, citing the seniors' housing wait list.
status_detail: CU-2026-03 approved (R26-109, unanimous); V-2026-05 approved with 1 stall per unit (R26-110, 5-2).
reasons: fairness-precedent: Seniors' housing need outweighs the green space in a transitional area. (Jac Siemens)
public: R.L. and other Friesen Avenue neighbours objected (green space since 1989, height, traffic); P.H. raised traffic.
notes: The 5-2 split concerned parking, not green space.

title: Mennonite Heritage Village subdivides highway frontage for commercial development
summary: Council approved the museum's application to subdivide about 31 acres along PTH 12 so commercial parcels can be developed, keeping existing uses.
status_detail: Subdivision 4451-2026-9245 approved (R26-114).

title: Williams Creek subdivision approved; playground left to cash-in-lieu and a later phase
summary: At the hearing for the 153-lot Williams Creek subdivision a resident asked where green space and playgrounds would go. The mayor said green space is handled in the development agreement; the developer said a dedication fee would be paid instead for this phase, with any park in Phase 2. Council approved the subdivision unanimously.
status_detail: Subdivision approved (R26-157); green-space dedication by fee for Phase 1, no playground planned in this phase.
reasons: study-first: Green space to be settled in the development agreement. (Mayor Earl Funk)
public: G.W. (resident) asked for immediate playgrounds and a full map of green space; S.B. asked about paths.

title: Accessible ramp allowed on city right-of-way at a Main Street bank
summary: Council let the Royal Bank install a removable accessible ramp on city right-of-way at 288 Main Street, likening it to patios on city land.
status_detail: Approved subject to annual review and permit (R26-189).

title: New Councillor Ron Falk appointed to the Jake Epp Library Board
summary: At the November 2026 inaugural meeting the mayor appointed new Councillor Ron Falk, a former school trustee, as council's library board representative, citing the city's commitment to literacy. Citizen appointments were deferred to November 17.
status_detail: Appointments ratified by resolution at the inaugural meeting.
notes: No minutes yet for Nov 3, 2026; mover/seconder of ratification from the chair's words.
